reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study has an overarching theme of the interplay between eFAS, Sae, and synovial infections. There is a lot of really interesting data. The paper is actually very hard to read and understand. The figure legends are not very helpful, and a ton of the needed information is buried in hard-to-find text and supplementary information. Many of the studies lack proper controls that lead to over interpretation of the data. At times, it dismisses already published studies that support the conclusions, but they are not referenced or mentioned in context.

There is a lot of problems with the statistics. Some panels have no statistics applied, while others have the wrong method applied. There are Mann-Whitney tests, one-way ANOVAs and two-way ANOVAs with no rational explanation as to why a particular method was used. A One-way ANOVA is not appropriate for comparing 2 treatments.

The introduction is devoid of relevant information on Staphylococcus aureus, Sae, and Fak.

Figure 1C does not indicate sample sizes and does not have error bars. Also, what is the dotted line?

Table S2 is supposed to contain Biofilm data. There are no definitions in the table to explain any of it. I assume B_ indicates biofilm but it is not explained. Figure 1F is equally difficult to understand.

One of the mutations shown for FakA in Figure S2C is labeled T171K, but the mutation shown does not match that.

Multiple papers connecting fatty acid accumulation, Sae, and FakA from different labs are not cited.

Mutations are not labeled conventionally; genetic mutants should be lowercase italics.

The FakA/Sae relationship studies in figure 2 agree with other published studies and this is not mentioned. It is known that FakA is upstream of SaeS.

It is really hard to believe that the only SNPs generated by evolution experiment would be in Sae or Fak. What other mutations were there? This information is severely lacking but could be highly relevant.

The complementation data is not clear. What promoters are used? If fnbA is regulated by SaeRS, then how could adding it back alone complement? Once you dig, you can find it. But this makes little sense when first reading. These details are too buried.

Lines 262-264. This does not make sense. If SaeRS is activated by FakA and the SaeP promoter is SaeR dependent, then why is it not lower in a fakA mutant? The same is true for fnb which is also activated by SaeRS. Shouldn’t all these transcripts be down in a fakA mutant? Also, the lines say that there is no difference in a fakA mutant with SF, but then goes on to say that Sae upregulation is FakA dependent. Also, the +SF levels are so low, is it even real expression?

Lines 268-272. This is counter to other published studies. Also, it says that 500 mM fatty acid was used. This is higher than the solubility of the fatty acid and seems impossible. Also, that level of 18:1 completely kills S. aureus.

Figure 4F. Do these concentrations of FasII inhibitors impact growth. This was not tested and decreased expression could just be the result growth inhibition and not Sae activity. Growth curves with these inhibitors should be added.

Figure 4H. How is it certain that this is lipid incorporation and not free fatty acid association? A fakA mutant should be used as a control in this experiment. Likewise, 4G should be done in the presence of a FasII inhibitor to show that it is specific to that pathway since acetate can enter metabolism through several metabolic pathways.

The split mCherry results in Fig S8 are not convincing. In some cases, there appears to be foci, but in additional cells, it looks like it is over most of the membrane surface.

Figure 6 needs to have colors matched for D-G for readability.

The data with UDA cannot be said to inhibit Fak. That data does not exist in its current. eFA incorporation requires more than just FakA/B. It also involves Pls proteins that may be the target. It is safe to say that it inhibits eFA incorporation but cannot be said that is it is a Fak inhibitor. That is an overstatement. In addition, some evidence exists that eFAs can enter FASII. Is it possible that this is part of what is happening? The data in Fig 7 does partially counter this last point. However, a fakA mutant would have strengthened these studies.

Heat maps lack actual data to validate them.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this work, Yu et al investigated the mechanism of bacterial infection-induced aggregation in the synovial fluid. Specifically, the authors used an array of experimental and computational tools to first establish the role of S. aureus SaeRS in aggregation and its regulation by Fak. This was done through directed evolution by several rounds of selection of S. aureus variants that were incapable of forming aggregates. The whole genome sequencing then allowed the authors to identify the mutations in two genes, SaeRS and Fak. Then, the extended study attempted to establish Fak as a therapeutic target and identified undecanoic acid (UDA) as an inhibitor for Fak system. This study is important given the lack of detailed understanding of the mechanisms of synovial joints lubrication and the infections targeting the synovial membrane/fluid and the tissues near the joints. The work seems to be comprehensive, and the findings are significant. A few points need to be addressed and clarified.

1) Composition of aggregates: It’s nice to see that the authors identified the primary proteins involved in forming the aggregates. Why is the 40kDa band not visible in the gel, but is prominent in the quantification? The Dispersin-B and DNase-I were used to rule out sugars/glycans and DNA. What about the role of (even in trace amounts) exRNA and lipids, especially during nucleation? Given the variety of proteins and other components involved, Fig. 3K will likely be more complicated. Perhaps include immunoglobin and adhesion proteins?

2) Fig. 4K lists the binding free energies and the caption says the calculation was done using AlphaFold3. While AF3 was used to model the complexes, the free energy calculation was done with the hawkDock, so this needs to be corrected. The MM/GBSA calculations are not very accurate but the relative values are still helpful, so this needs to be discussed/acknowledged.

3) The assays showing direct interactions between FloA-SaeSR are novel. However, the simulations do not seem to provide much insight. A few microseconds are typical for more accurate all-atom simulations and ns-timescales are inadequate for CG simulations to observe any meaningful scaffolding or interactions. Given that tens or hundreds of microseconds can easily be done, it’s unclear why the authors chose CG and not take advantage of the access to longer timescales. Still, free diffusion of the proteins in such simulations is prohibitively slow and unlikely to yield meaningful complexes. A better strategy would be to also include pre-formed complexes (in addition to free proteins) obtained with AF3 or docking and set up the simulations.

4) What about other proteins associated with FMMs (e.g. IsdF, PBP2a)? Do they have any role, or form co-complex with SaeSR/FloA?

5) Given the importance of UDA as potential therapeutic target of FakB1, an all-atom MD would help more accurately position the substrate and identify the interactions. This is because docking is unlikely to produce an accurate pose especially when docked to a modeled or substrate-free apo structure.

6) Fix typos e.g. (“By review published FMMs …”   “Reviewing the published FMMs…”)

7) The simulations are generally expected to be deposited to data sharing sites such as Zenodo.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. Below are our point-by-point responses to each comment. All corresponding revisions in the manuscript have been highlighted in yellow for the reviewers' convenience.

Reviewer1
Comments from Reviewer 1: I have carefully reviewed the manuscript by Yu et al., which investigates the link between biofilm formation and the ability to establish synovial infections through a directed evolution approach. This study builds on previous findings and I find little additional insight beyond what has already been published in the field. Furthermore, the manuscript presents technical and conceptual flaws, as well as writting issues, which hinder its clarity and overall impact.

Author response: Thank you very much for your detailed review and for the time and effort you have invested in evaluating our manuscript. We appreciate your constructive critiques, which have enabled us to correct several experimental and technical flaws and to perform additional experiments that strengthen our work.
We respectfully disagree with the assessment that our study lacks new insight. Our study builds upon previous literature but goes beyond mere replication of prior research. We believe this impression may stem from a conceptual misunderstanding regarding the distinction between synovial aggregation and biofilms. Aggregates typically arise in highly dynamic fluids—e.g., synovial fluid and blood flow, which makes it critical in the pathogenesis of septic arthritis. Biofilms, in contrast, form on relatively static, abiotic surfaces such as medical implants. The detailed distinct behaviors were provided in the point-by-point response below.
Regarding the methodological concerns you raised, we have conducted additional experiments to enhance rigor and provide robust support for our conclusions. We have also revised the manuscript to correct the nomenclature issues you identified. Below, we address each of your specific comments point by point.

Comments from Reviewer 1: The authors identify mutations in saeS and fakA that inhibit bacterial aggregation. However, the authors conceptually distinguishes bacterial aggregation from biofilm formation, despite these are closely related processes in Staphylococcus aureus. Unlike in other bacterial species, biofilm formation in S. aureus is primarily driven by adhesin production and cellular aggregation rather than extracellular matrix synthesis. This fundamental misconception affects the interpretation of the experimental results.

Author response: We thank the reviewer for the comments. We consider synovial aggregation and biofilm formation to be closely related but distinct bacterial behaviors with different phenotypic manifestations. Also, we disagree that synovial aggregation was part of the biofilm formation. First, biofilm is a surface-attached bacterial community, while aggregates are the non-attached floating bacterial population. This means biofilm was always seen in medical implant surfaces, while the aggregates are always present in flowing body fluids, especially in joint spaces and bloodstream. Secondly, the size of a mature aggregate (1-10 mm in diameter, Revised Figure 1A-B) is obviously tens to hundreds larger than the biofilm size (~100 μm thick). Thirdly, synovial aggregation happened rapidly. It forms small aggregates within 30 minutes and matures within 4-6 hours, depending on the concentration of synovial fluid (Revised Figure 1C). In contrast, a typical biofilm requires overnight culture for maturation (Moormeier et al., 2014). Lastly, as demonstrated by a previous study (Perez & Patel, 2015), S. aureus with weak biofilm-forming capacity can still exhibit robust aggregation ability, indicating that the underlying formation mechanisms are different, at least not entirely identical. In our study, we tested the correlation between biofilm-forming capacity and aggregation propensity across 152 clinical isolates from orthopedic infections and found no significant correlation between the two phenotypes (Revised Figure 1F). This again confirms that these two phenotypes are independent of each other. Over the past decade, numerous groups have investigated aggregates as a separate phenotype, and the distinction is now widely accepted by experts in the field (Bidossi et al., 2020; Dastgheyb et al., 2015; Knott et al., 2021; Staats et al., 2022). These studies lead us to believe that past conclusions based on biofilms cannot be directly applied to synovial aggregation. We hope the provided evidence from the published literature and our experimental data could change the impression of synovial aggregation. We have also added this information to the introduction part to provide relevant background (Line 58-61).

Revised Figure 1(A-C, F). (A) Representative fluorescence images of GFP-S. aureus forming aggregates from 0-3 hours since inoculated into 20% human synovial fluid. (B) Representative images of S. aureus aggregation in 20% synovial fluid after 0, 4, 5, and 6 hours of incubation. (C) S. aureus aggregates diameter growth curve measured over a continuous 12-hour observation period (n = 5/time point). The dashed horizontal line at y = 10 µm indicates the size threshold beyond which phagocytes lose the ability to internalize particles. (F) Histograms and correlation analysis of proteinaceous biofilm, polysaccharide biofilm formation abilities, and aggregation ability for 152 clinical strains. Correlation was analyzed with spearman method. i,iii,vi: histogram distributions for polysaccharide biofilm(i), proteinaceous biofilm(iii), and aggregation ability(vi). ii, iv, v: correlation plot between polysaccharide and proteinaceous biofilm(ii), polysaccharide biofilm and aggregation ability(iv), proteinaceous biofilm and aggregation ability(v).

Comments from Reviewer 1: Additionally, the selection conditions to identify non-aggregating mutants introduce a significant limitation: while these non-aggregating mutants fail to establish infections, the study does not establish a direct causal link between biofilm-defective evolved strains and infection-defective strains. This means, any mutation affecting growth, metabolism, cell wall organization, adhesin production, or membrane integrity would likely impair bacterial aggregation and infection, making it difficult to isolate specific effects. The authors need to demonstrate this causal effect to move forward.

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful critique regarding the potential pleiotropic effects of sae/fak mutations and the need to establish a direct causal link between aggregation defects and the observed infection deficiencies. The reviewer highlights the inherent challenge in definitively isolating the specific contribution of aggregation when sae/fak regulates a broad regulon encompassing virulence factors, metabolism, and cell wall organization. To address the specific contribution of the aggregation phenotype to infection success, we presented multiple lines of evidence throughout the original manuscript to prove this causal link.
1. Clinical Correlation: We observed a significant enhancement in aggregation capacity among S. aureus clinical isolates specifically recovered from joint infections compared to isolates from non-joint sources. This association suggests a potential role for robust aggregation in the context of joint infection pathogenesis (Figure 1E).
Figure 1E. Violin plot illustrating the difference in aggregation ability between strains of joint infection (n = 41) and non-joint infection group (n = 111).
2. Direct Phenotypic Impact in vitro: Critically, we directly compared antibiotic tolerance and immune evasion capabilities between aggregated and non-aggregated states of the same bacterial strains. Aggregated bacteria exhibited substantially higher resistance to clinically relevant antibiotics compared to their planktonic counterparts. Moreover, bacterial aggregates were significantly more resistant to phagocytosis and killing by immune cells. (Figure 1LM, Figure S1F-H)
Revised Figure 1L-M. CFU count results of human PMN/ RAW264.7 co-cultured with S. aureus of varying aggregation abilities in culture medium with/without 20% synovial fluid (indicated with gray shadow) (n=5/group). Statistical analysis is by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test for pairwise comparison. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.005, and ****p < 0.0001.
Revised Figure S1 (F-H). Quantification for survived clinical isolates of varying aggregation abilities incubated with/without 20% synovial fluids containing gentamicin (5 μg/mL) or vancomycin (5 μg/mL). n = 5/group. Statistical analysis by one-way ANOVA followed with Tukey’s post-hoc test. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.005, and ****p < 0.0001.
These controlled experiments demonstrated that the aggregated state itself, irrespective of the other effects controlled by the sae regulon, conferred significant advantages against major host defenses encountered during infection. We have explicitly stated it in the revised manuscript (line 121-125)
3. Exploring the specific effect of fnbAB in vivo: To specifically isolate the causal effect of aggregation on infection. We demonstrated that fbnA/B were critical for synovial aggregation (Revised Figure 3G-K). Then, the fnbAB knock-out strain was used to establish a septic arthritis mouse model. Result showed that fnbAB significantly reduced the infection burden though not to the ΔsaeRS levels in early stage (indicating that sae regulates additional factors contributing to virulence, Figure S5C-D). This partial but significant infection defect, specifically by restoring the aggregation machinery, provides compelling evidence that the loss of aggregation contributes substantially to the infection defect observed in the ΔsaeRS mutant.
Figure 3G-K. (G). Adhesins were controlled by a tetracycline-inducible promoter. S. aureus was stimulated with/without anhydrotetracycline (1 µg/mL) to induce the adhesin overexpression. n = 5/group. (H-I) Aggregation assay for USA300 of different genotypes in 20% synovial fluid (H), and the quantitative results (I). n = 6/group. (J) Aggregation assay for USA300 of different genotypes in the indicated medium. (K) Illustration for the mechanism of S. aureus adhesins and host extracellular proteins contributing to synovial aggregation. Statistical analysis is by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post-tests versus values in controls. Error bars show the mean ± SD, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.005, and ****p < 0.0001.
Supplementary Figure S5C-D. (C)Bacterial burden for mice knee infected with WT, △fnbAB, △saeRS. Seven mice(14 knees) per group. (D)Representative immunofluorescence images for knee joint tissue sections stained with polyclonal antibodies against S. aureus (Green). Statistical analysis is by one-way ANOVA Dunnett’s post-tests versus values in controls. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.005, and ****p < 0.0001.
While we fully acknowledge that saeRS regulates multiple pathways beyond aggregation that likely contribute to joint infection success, the convergent evidence from clinical isolates, controlled in vitro functional assays on the aggregation phenotype itself, and the partial in vivo infection defect by fnbAB mutation strongly supports our conclusion that enhanced aggregation is a key mechanism by which sae promotes S. aureus joint infection, primarily by conferring resistance to antibiotics and immune clearance.
Our study focused specifically on dissecting the contribution of the aggregation phenotype, and the data presented collectively support its significant role. Exploring the relative contributions of other saeRS-regulated pathways is indeed an important avenue for future research beyond the scope of this current work. We hope this clarification supports the causal link between aggregation and infection.

Comments from Reviewer 1: The methodological approaches present critical shortcomings. For instance, the two-hybrid system lacks essential controls, including plasmid-free conditions, quantitative Miller unit measurements, and both positive and negative controls. The molecular dynamics experiments are limited in temporal scale and lack proper theoretical validation. Similarly, the fluorescence microscopy experiments do not include necessary controls to confirm that the observed signals are not artifacts caused by protein aggregation. Moreover, the manuscript does not address whether the fluorescent protein fusions retain functionality. These examples illustrate broader experimental issues, highlighting fundamental methodological flaws throughout the study.

Author response: We thank the reviewer for constructive suggestions.
1. For the bacterial two-hybrid (B2H) experiments, the reviewer noted the lack of corresponding positive and negative controls as well as plasmid-free conditions. Since the FloA-FloA interaction has been previously confirmed (García-Fernández et al., 2017; Ukleja et al., 2024), we used it and the ZIP interaction as the positive control. Additionally, we included a plasmid-free condition as a blank control (Revised Figure 5A-B). A vector control, either in combination with plasmids or alone, was included. As per your suggestion, we also incorporated quantitative measurements to quantify the strength of protein interaction (Revised Figure 5C). The results demonstrated a strong interaction between FloA and SaeS. We have improved the presentation of the experimental results by labeling the corresponding control groups and providing detailed annotations in the figure legend for clarity.
Revised figure 5(A-C) (A) Bacterial two-hybrid (BTH) assay results. Membrane proteins (SaeS, P, Q, and FloA) were expressed as prey (Vector: T25) and bait (Vector: T18C) proteins in E. coli (BTH101). Protein interaction activates lacZ expression, leading to the degradation of X-Gal (blue stain). (B) E. coli (BTH101) transfected with a single plasmid was grown on LB agar to serve as a control. (C) Quantification of interaction efficiency in a β-galactosidase assay. Red box: the ZIP interaction was set as a positive control. Green box: BTH101 carrying no plasmid was set as the blank control. Blue box: BTH101 carrying plasmid vectors was set as the negative control. Z(ZIP), A(FloA), P(SaeP), Q(SaeQ), S(SaeS),V(Vector). (n = 3/group)
2. To address the concern about simulation timescales, we have extended our CG simulations from the original 1000 ns to 5000 ns (5 µs). Extended simulations confirm the stability of the protein complex (SaeS RMSD reached a plateau at ~5.0 nm after 1 μs; FloA RMSD reached a plateau at 8nm after 4 μs (Revised Supplementary Figure S8B-D). Furthermore, we fully acknowledge that computational predictions necessitate validation through biological experiments. To this end, we have incorporated new co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) data demonstrating a direct physical interaction between FloA-3xFLAG and SaeS-6xHIS (Revised Figure 5D). Specifically, we co-expressed SaeS-3xFLAG and FloA-6xHIS in USA300 through a plasmid. Anti-HIS magnetic beads were used to immunoprecipitate FloA-6xHIS, and the resulting pull-down product was immunoblotted with an anti-FLAG antibody to detect associated SaeS-3xFLAG. Our results clearly show that FloA binds to SaeS, providing robust biochemical validation that supports the interaction observed in our extensive coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics simulations. This was included in the revised manuscript (Line 376-380)
Revised Supplementary Figure S8 B-D (B) Computational molecular dynamic modulation of FloA and SaeS interaction on the cell membrane (blue: FloA, purple: SaeS). (C) The curves of the total solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) of FLOA and SAES proteins over time. The vertical axis represents the solvent-accessible surface area at the corresponding moment. (D) The RMSD (Root Mean Square Deviation) curve of the SaeS/FloA protein over time.
Revised Figure 5D: Co-IP and immunoblot analysis of USA300 overexpressing FloA-6xHIS and SaeS-3xFLAG. SDS-PAGE result shows that the protein contents were comparable among the three groups.
3. Regarding the specificity of our fluorescence microscopy data. We fully agree that rigorous controls are vital to distinguish true biological signals from potential artifacts like non-specific signal or protein aggregation. To directly test whether the observed split-mCherry fluorescence signals could arise from non-specific protein aggregation rather than true protein-protein interaction within FMMs, we employed a functional disruption control using a well-characterized FMM inhibitor (Zaragozic acid)(García-Fernández et al., 2017). We treated bacterial cells expressing the split-mCherry fusion proteins with zaragozic acid. Upon inhibitor treatment, we observed a specific dissolution of the fluorescent foci (Revised Supplementary Figure S9B). This result is consistent with the established mechanism of this inhibitor and demonstrates that the split-mCherry fluorescence signal is dependent on intact, functional FMMs. If the signals were merely due to non-specific protein aggregation (unrelated to FMM localization), they would be expected to persist despite FMM disruption. The inhibitor-induced loss of signal, therefore, provides strong evidence that the observed fluorescence represents specific protein interaction/localization within FMMs, not aggregation artifacts.
Revised Supplementary Figure S9B. High resolution confocal images for USA300 expression NtmCherry-FloA and SaeS-CtmCherry treated with/without zaragozic acid. NtmCherry-FloA: N-terminal split mCherry was fused to the N-terminal of the FloA protein. SaeS-CtmCherry: C-terminal split mCherry was fused to the C-terminal of SaeS proteins. FloA-NtmCherry: N-terminal split mCherry was fused to the C-terminal of the FloA protein, as a negative control. Negative control: USA300 expression of FloA-NtmCherry and SaeS-CtmCherry.
4. Regarding the functional validation of our fluorescent protein fusions (FloA and SaeS). We agree that confirming the functionality of tagged proteins is essential, and we have now performed additional experiments to address this concern comprehensively. Our FloA-splitmCherry fusion construct (tagged at the N-terminus) was designed based on established literature demonstrating that FloA retains its ability to localize to functional membrane microdomains (FMMs) regardless of tag placement (N- or C-terminus) (Koch et al., 2017). Also, the full-length GFP tagged to FloA was proven to retain its function according to the data from their published literature (García-Fernández et al., 2017). To rigorously confirm that FloA-splitmCherry retains its function, we constructed a FloA-FloA splitmCherry reporter plasmid. Then treat the S. aureus expressing FloA-FloA splitmCherry reporter plasmid with zaragozic acid (FMM inhibitor). Consistent with previous reports on native FloA function (García-Fernández et al., 2017), we observed a complete disappearance of the fluorescent foci upon zaragozic acid treatment (Revised Supplementary Figure S9C). This result demonstrates that FloA-splitmCherry retains its essential scaffolding function and responds appropriately to FMM perturbation.
Revised Supplementary Figure S9C. High resolution confocal images for USA300 expression NtmCherry-FloA and FloA-CtmCherry treated with/without zaragozic acid. NtmCherry-FloA: split mCherry was fused to the N-terminal of the FloA protein. FloA-CtmCherry: C-terminal split mCherry was fused to the C-terminal of FloA proteins.
SaeS is a histidine kinase central to the SaeRS two-component system, regulating the expression of key virulence factors (e.g., hemolysins). A typical phenotype of the SaeRS mutant was the absence of hemolysis ring grown on sheep blood agar. To test if SaeS-splitmCherry retains its signaling function, we complemented the △saeRS strain with a plasmid expressing SaeS-splitRFP and wild-type SaeR. The result showed that SaeRS::pSaeR/SaeS-splitRFP restored the hemolysis ring. Indicating that the splitRFP tag did not impair the protein function (Revised Supplementary Figure S9D).
Revised Supplementary Figure S9D. Representative images for USA300-ΔsaeRS expressing saeR, and saeS-splitmCherry (or saeS) grown on blood agar plates. Hemolysis rings were absent in ΔsaeRS and ΔsaeRS transfected with only saeR.

Comments from Reviewer 1: There are also recurring issues with nomenclature throughout the text. In molecular biology, the symbol Δ denotes a gene knockout, not a protein deletion, which is an impossible task to make (e.g., ΔsaeS correctly refers to a strain lacking the saeS gene). Gene names should be written in lowercase italics, with an uppercase final letter when denoting a specific locus, whereas protein names should begin with an uppercase letter and not be italicized (e.g., the saeS gene encodes the SaeS protein). The manuscript inconsistently applies these conventions, often misusing Δ to refer to proteins, which is incorrect. It is incorrect because proteins cannot be knocked out; just genes can be knocked out. Additionally, bacterial species names should always be italicized (e.g., line 330).

Author response: We sincerely appreciate your meticulous attention to nomenclature standards and apologize for our oversight in adhering to these critical formatting conventions. In response to your suggestion, we have gone through the text carefully and fixed all those issues:
1.Δ symbol is now strictly used before gene names to indicate gene knockouts.
2. Genes are presented in lowercase italics, and proteins in plain text begin with an uppercase letter.
3. Species names are now properly italicized everywhere.

Comments from Reviewer 1: Regarding the biological findings, many of the conclusions presented in this study have already been extensively documented by other research groups. The role of the SaeSR system in adhesin production and biofilm formation, independent of ica, has been well established (for a review in the field, see PMID: 28581360). Similarly, the influence of fatty acids and Fak on SaeSR activity has been explored in detail by Brinsmade’s laboratory (e.g., PMID: 36135382, 36778227, 38366323, 39382300). The connection between membrane microdomains (FMMs) and SaeS activity has also been previously reported (PMID: 39382300, 34370508).

Author response: Thank you for reviewing our manuscript. While it is true that the regulation of sae by fak and fatty acids has been previously reported (as cited in our paper), our study expanded previous findings in a disease-specific environment since all prior studies were conducted in vitro. Also, the connections between SaeS and FMMs were not experimentally verified yet in the previous report mentioned by the reviewer. Below, we would like to highlight the key innovations of our study in detail:
1. Dissecting genetic regulators for synovial aggregation using a non-biased method.
Instead of a hypothesis-driven experiment design, we adopted a directed evolution method to dissect regulators of synovial aggregation in S. aureus. This method allows S. aureus to evolve into a non-aggregating mutant, enabling the identification of causative genetic mutations through genome sequencing. This method applies to other pathogens known to aggregate in synovial fluid (e.g., S. epidermidis).
As for the biological findings of our study, we disagree that conclusions from biofilm can be directly applied to synovial aggregates, for they exhibit different bacterial behavior as discussed thoroughly above. Moreover, the literature provided by the reviewer just reflects the biological findings of our work. As noted in the review (PMID: 28581360), a complex of adhesins (MSCRAMMs, FnbA/B, SasG et.al. ) and extracellular proteins(PSM, α-hemolysin) contributed to the formation of ica-independent biofilm. These adhesins and proteins are precisely regulated by a complex network of regulators (agrAC, saeRS, sigB, mgrA, rot protein, et.al. ). In this work, we demonstrated that saeRS plays the dominant regulatory role in synovial fluid, emphasizing its unique importance in this specific clinical context—a finding never reported before. Besides, the saeRS mutation totally “abolished” rather than “reduced” aggregation. That means saeRS (or its epistatic regulator) as a promising therapy target for septic arthritis—another unreported insight.
2. Mechanistic elucidation of Fak/fatty acid regulation of SaeRS via FMMs remodeling
Although the connection between fak and sae activity has been established in previous studies, the precise mechanism by which fak/fatty acids regulate sae remains unclear. In this study, we hypothesize that fak/fatty acids modulate sae activity through FMMs (functional membrane microdomain) remodeling.
The reviewer noted that the relationship between FMMs and SaeS has been previously suggested (Alqahtani et al., 2024; Sanson et al., 2021). However, upon careful reading of the references, we found that these prior studies only proposed speculative hypotheses based on previously published FMMs proteomics datasets (García-Fernández et al., 2017), with no subsequent mechanistic investigations and experimental verification. Here, we experimentally demonstrated that fak regulates sae by altering its FMMs architecture. Since the referenced studies merely presented conjectures without experimental evidence for sae localization in FMMs or fak-mediated sae regulation via raft structural changes, our work significantly advances prior theoretical hypotheses by providing robust experimental validation.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript “Elucidating the Role of Staphylococcus aureus Fatty Acid Metabolism in SaeRS-Mediated Aggregation and Pathogenesis of Joint Infections,” Yu et al report a role for the SaeRS two-component system in aggregation of staphylococci within synovial fluid. The authors first demonstrate that highly aggregating clinical strains from MSKI patients lead to greater disease pathogenesis in a murine model of septic arthritis (higher CFUs, more gait disturbance, etc). The split mCherry results in Fig S8 are not convincing. In some cases, there appears to be foci, but in additional cells, it looks like it is over most of the membrane surface.

Author response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this valid concern regarding the apparent inconsistency in the localization patterns observed in the original Figure S8.
The variation in mCherry signal distribution—ranging from distinct foci to a more diffuse membrane pattern—was primarily due to limitations in our initial imaging conditions. Our high-resolution confocal microscope uses an exceptionally thin optical section, making the focal plane extremely sensitive. In the original images, high bacterial density resulted in many cells being out of the focal plane; some were dead or lysed, leading to blurred fluorescence and inaccurate localization that manifested as a diffuse membrane signal.
To address this, we have repeated the imaging under optimized conditions: we used mid-log phase cultures, significantly reduced the bacterial density during slide preparation, and increased the signal threshold to minimize background noise. These adjustments allow for clearer visualization of individual bacteria in the focal plane, as shown in the Revised Figure S9 provided below.
Furthermore, to confirm that the observed foci represent functional FMM structures, we included an additional control experiment using a specific FMM inhibitor. Treatment with this inhibitor resulted in the complete disappearance of the fluorescent foci, confirming that the foci signal indeed corresponds to FMM.
As a positive control, we constructed the FloA-FloA splitmCherry reporter plasmid. Then treating S. aureus expressing FloA-FloA splitmCherry reporter plasmid with zaragozic acid (FMM inhibitor). Consistent with previous reports on native FloA function (García-Fernández et al., 2017), we observed a complete disappearance of the fluorescent foci upon zaragozic acid treatment (Revised Supplementary Figure S9C).
We believe these corrections and additional validation significantly strengthen the reliability of the results. Thank you again for the critical comment, which has helped us improve the quality of our data.

In addition, some evidence exists that eFAs can enter FASII. Is it possible that this is part of what is happening? The data in Fig 7 does partially counter this last point. However, a fakA mutant would have strengthened these studies.

Author response: We are delighted that our data have provided further insights and inspired additional discussion. Our data in Figure 7 suggest that eFA enables S. aureus to be resistant to the anti-FASII antibiotics. This result agrees with previous literature that anti-FASII were less effective within the host environment because pathogens could bypass the FASII by incorporating environmental eFA(Morvan et al., 2016). To our knowledge, fak was the only pathway that S. aureus used to incorporate eFA. However, the reviewer noted that fatty acids were proven to enter the FASII system and undergo elongation (Parsons, Frank, et al., 2014). Therefore, as suggested by the reviewer, we tested the fakA mutant strain its resistance to anti-FASII antibiotics in the presence of eFA/synovial fluid (Revised Figure 7D-E). The results showed that the fakA mutant did not show an increase in resistance to anti-FASII antibiotics in the presence of eFA/synovial fluid (Revised Figure 7D-E). These data further strengthened previous studies that eFAs can bypass FASII through the fak system. However, this does not mean that eFAs cannot enter FASII. Because, as an inhibitor for FASII, AFN1252 and Triclosan block the elongation process if eFA enters the FASII. Therefore, based on these literatures and additional experimental data, we carefully concluded that eFAs can bypass FASII through the fak system, but cannot exclude the possibility that eFA can enter FASII.

Author response: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful comments regarding the simulations. It is true that all-atom simulation and longer simulation times provide more convincing evidence. All-atom simulation is typically adopted for small molecular interactions with proteins and usually. However, the simulation in our project involves protein-protein interaction, and the simulation was constructed within the bacterial membrane, a non-typical simulation environment. The all-atom simulation for such a large and atypical system requires large computing resources, which is unreachable for our group.
To address the concern about simulation timescales, we have extended our CG simulations from the original 1000 ns to 5000 ns (5 µs). You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Staphylococcus aureus can form aggregates within human synovial fluid, contributing to joint infections that are resistant to conventional therapies. However, the regulatory pathways underlying this process remain unclear. Here, we reveal that the S. aureus two-component system saeRS contributes to synovial aggregation by controlling the expression of fibrinectin-binding proteins A and B (FnbA/B), which bind to human fibrinogen and cause aggregation. We further demonstrate that the fatty acid kinase (fak) system is the primary regulator for SaeS activity under host conditions. Mechanistically, fak is epistatic to saeRS by scavenging exogenous fatty acids and altering the localization of SaeS into functional membrane microdomains (FMMs), which are essential for SaeS function. We also identify that undecanoic acid (UDA) is capable of inhibiting the fak pathway, demonstrating its efficacy and potential applicability in treating joint infections. Altogether, these findings highlight the fak-saeRS axis as a potential therapeutic target for joint infections and underscore UDA as a promising treatment for these infections.

---

## Introduction

Joint infections, either native or prosthetic, represent a formidable clinical challenge in musculoskeletal medicine1. Left untreated, joint infections can lead to irreversible joint damage, chronic pain, functional impairment, and even amputation2,3. Therefore, accurate diagnosis and prompt intervention are urgently needed to mitigate the potentially devastating consequences associated with joint destruction and systemic spread of infection. Although substantial research efforts have advanced our understanding of joint infections1,4, persistent challenges in clinical management and evolving microbial resistance patterns underscore the need for continued refinement of therapeutic strategies and molecular-level understanding of host–pathogen interactions. Further research remains crucial to address critical knowledge gaps and translate mechanistic insights into improved patient outcomes.

Staphylococcus aureus is the primary causative pathogen of septic arthritis and periprosthetic joint infections5,6. Notably, S. aureus strongly tends to aggregate within the synovial fluid, which promotes persistent infection and treatment resistance7. Although closely related, synovial aggregation and biofilm formation are distinct phenomena with different phenotypic manifestations. Synovial aggregates form quickly and develop much larger amounts of biomass. The aggregation process is believed to involve a sophisticated interplay between host and bacterial factors. Host molecules such as fibrinogen and fibronectin serve as substrates for bacterial adhesion via microbial surface proteins such as ClfA/B and FnbA/B8. Despite significant research efforts, the key regulator of this aggregation process and its specific impact on infection outcomes remain incompletely understood, highlighting a critical gap in pathogenesis knowledge. Therefore, elucidating the precise mechanism underlying synovial aggregation is essential for developing targeted therapeutic strategies.

S. aureus transcription is tightly controlled by two-component systems (TCSs). In particular, the saeRS TCS regulates the expression of more than 20 surface-associated adhesins and secreted virulence factors, such as hla (ɑ-haemolysin), coa (coagulase), nuc (thermonuclease), and several proteases9,10. The activity of saeRS is modulated by various factors: it is positively activated by fatty acid kinase (fak) and codY, as well as by the presence of human neutrophil peptides, calprotectin, or hydrogen peroxide. In contrast, free fatty acids inhibit saeRS activity11,12. Notably, fak dysfunction significantly downregulates saeRS, underscoring a close functional relationship13,14. fak is a two-component enzyme that utilizes exogenous fatty acids to generate acyl-phosphate for phospholipid synthesis and cell membrane construction15–17. The fak system consists of a kinase domain protein (FakA) that phosphorylates a fatty acid enveloped by a fatty acid binding protein (FakB1/2)18,19. Parsons et al.15. proposed that fak might activate saeRS activity through phosphorylation of the SaeS protein. However, this was not true in a previous study20. Yet the mechanism by which fak affects saeRS activity has not been determined. The relationships among eFA, fak, and sae need to be thoroughly explored.

Here, the critical role of S. aureus saeRS in synovial aggregation, a key pathogenic mechanism in joint infections, is elucidated. We determined that saeRS activity is regulated by the fak system within the host environment. Mechanistically, fak regulates the localization of the SaeS histidine kinase within functional membrane microdomains (FMMs). Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the high adaptability of S. aureus to the synovial fluid environment to facilitate its pathogenesis. Finally, we identified undecanoic acid (UDA), a medium-chain fatty acid (C11:0) capable of inhibiting the Fak system. UDA effectively inhibits S. aureus aggregation and enhances the efficacy of anti-FASII antibiotics, suggesting its potential as a promising adjuvant therapy for joint infections.

---

## Results

S. aureus synovial aggregation contributes to joint infections
Bacterial synovial aggregation is fundamentally distinct from biofilm, as it rapidly surpasses the phagocytosis size (>10µm in diameter21) within one hour and matures within a few hours (Fig. 1A–C). Currently, no evidence directly demonstrates the contribution of synovial aggregation ability to the severity of septic arthritis. To address this gap, we analysed S. aureus strains from patients with musculoskeletal infections (Fig. 1D). The isolates were classified into joint-involved and joint-not-involved groups (n=41 for JI; n=111 for N-JI). By quantifying their aggregation and biofilm formation abilities, we found that compared with the N-JI group, the JI group presented greater aggregation ability, whereas no difference in biofilm formation ability was observed between the JI and N-JI groups (Fig. 1E, Supplementary Data 1 and 2, and Fig. S1A, B). Moreover, the aggregation ability was not correlated with biofilm ability (Fig. 1F), indicating that aggregation was an independent factor strongly associated with joint infections.

To further verify this, we selected the five strains with the greatest aggregation ability (H1–H5) and the five with the lowest aggregation ability (L1–L5) to establish a knee joint infection mouse model. First, the growth of the representative strains did not differ when cultured in 20% synovial fluid (Fig. S1C). Each mouse was subsequently infected with a high-aggregating isolate at the right knee and a low-aggregating isolate at the left knee. The results revealed that mice infected with high-aggregating S. aureus exhibited more severe infections with greater cartilage impairment (Fig. 1G), limited joint movement (Fig. 1H–J), and greater bacterial burden (Fig. 1K). When cocultured with immune cells or treated with antibiotics, high-aggregating isolates showed significant increases in resistance to immune cell killing (~twofold, Fig. 1L, M), phagocytosis (~twofold, Fig. S1D, E), and antibiotic killing compared with their unaggregated state (100–1000-fold, Fig. S1F–H). The phenotypic difference between the aggregated and unaggregated states of the same strain indicates that synovial aggregation behaviour, rather than other genetic factors, helps the bacteria evade both the host immune response and antimicrobial therapies. This provides a strong link between aggregation and joint infections.

Directed evolution revealed that synovial aggregation depends on SaeRS activity
Our analysis revealed no significant correlation between biofilm formation and aggregation in S. aureus, suggesting that distinct mechanisms govern aggregation. This prompted us to investigate the genetic pathways underlying synovial aggregation. We performed directed evolution by selecting planktonic S. aureus populations within SF (synovial fluid) (Fig. 2A). S. aureus strain USA300 was initially exposed to SF for aggregation; unaggregated cells were then isolated from the planktonic fraction and grown overnight in tryptic soy broth (TSB) before they were reintroduced into SF for the next round of aggregation. The evolution was repeated until aggregation was no longer observable (Fig. 2B). As anticipated, the evolved population exhibited increased susceptibility to antibiotics and reduced resistance to immune cell killing (Figs. 2C and S2A, B). Notably, the evolved population also showed a progressive loss of haemolysis rings on sheep blood agar plates (Fig. 2D). We confirmed that the haemolysis-ring-negative colonies were all nonaggregating (Fig. 2D) and that the mutation was irreversible, even when the cells were cultured for several passages. Whole-genome sequencing of the randomly selected nonaggregating isolates revealed mutations in the saePQRS or fakA locus (Figs. 2E and S2C).

The sae locus, encoding the saeRS TCS and auxiliary saePQ factors, is central to the activation of key virulence factors and adhesins, with a link to fak, as shown in previous studies14,15. We confirmed the roles of fakA and saeRS in aggregation by testing their mutants in SF; ΔsaeRS and ΔfakA were nonaggregating but were restored upon complementation (Fig. 2F). Consistent with these findings, both saeRS and fakA mutants exhibited reduced resistance to phagocytosis and heightened sensitivity to antibiotics and immune cell-mediated killing in SF (Figs. 2G–H and S2D–F). We also demonstrated that bacterial growth was not impaired for the mutants when they were grown in 20% SF (Fig. S2G). We next investigated whether fakA influences aggregation via saeRS by complementing ΔfakA with saeRS (ΔfakA::psaeRS) and ΔsaeRS with fakA (ΔsaeRS::pfakA). Notably, aggregation was restored in only the ΔfakA::psaeRS strain but not in the ΔsaeRS::pfakA strain (Fig. 2I). Furthermore, fakA knockout significantly decreased saeRS transcription, suggesting that fakA is epistatic to saeRS (Fig. 2J, K). These results agree with those of previously published studies13–15.

We subsequently repeated the directed evolution experiment with high-aggregating clinical strains (H1–H5). The results revealed an anticipated decrease in aggregation ability (Fig. S2H). Subsequent genome sequencing revealed DEL/SNPs in the fakA, fakB1, and saePQRS loci (Fig. S2I and Supplementary Data 3), which further supports our findings that the fak–sae axis contributes to synovial aggregation. Molecular docking analysis of FakA binding with FakB1/2 revealed that the SNPs led to changes in amino acids that were critical for binding function, possibly explaining the dysfunction of the fak system (FakA[R246, E311, R314, F422, E532, E548], FakB1[202~209]; Fig. S3A–D and Supplementary Data 3).

FnbA/B-fibrinogen interaction is the key step in synovial aggregation
To further explore the mechanism of aggregation, we first confirmed that the aggregates were primarily composed of proteins. This conclusion was based on the observation that treatment with dispersin-B, DNase-I, RNase-H, and lipase did not inhibit aggregation and that even the nucleation step was not affected (Fig. S4A, B), whereas proteinase K significantly inhibited aggregation (Fig. S4A), suggesting that proteins play a critical role in synovial aggregation. SDS–PAGE of the aggregates revealed enrichment of proteins at 60 and 80 kDa (Fig. 3A, B). Proteomic analysis of aggregates revealed these enriched proteins as immunoglobulins, keratins, fibrinogen, complement proteins, lipoproteins, and fibronectin (Fig. 3C and Supplementary Data 4).

To determine which bacterial adhesins interact with these proteins, we first identified saeRS-regulated genes from a large S. aureus transcriptome dataset with a machine learning method (Fig. 3D)22,23. Among the 34 genes predicted to be downstream of saeR, 23 were verified to be downregulated in the ΔsaeRS RNA-seq data, and 8 were adhesins (Figs. 3E and S5B and Supplementary Data 5). Complementing ΔsaeRS with each of the eight adhesins and inducing overexpression with anhydrotetracycline revealed that only fnbA/B restored aggregation (Figs. 3F, G and S5A). Moreover, the fnbA or fnbB mutant did not completely abolish aggregation, whereas the double mutant eliminated aggregation, suggesting that both fnbA and fnbB are essential for aggregation (Fig. 3H, I).

FnbA/B are proteins that bind fibronectin and fibrinogen24. We then explored how fibronectin and fibrinogen contribute to aggregation. The incubation of S. aureus with fibrinogen, but not fibronectin, induced the adhesin overexpression, which was abolished in the ΔfnbAB strain, indicating that fibrinogen mediates aggregation through binding with FnbA/B adhesins (Fig. 3J, K). We also tested the pathogenesis of fnbAB in a mouse model of joint sepsis. Immunofluorescence detection of S. aureus revealed that the bacterial aggregates around the joint were reduced in the ΔfnbAB and ΔsaeRS groups, although the difference in bacterial burden between the ΔfnbAB and WT groups was not as significant as that in the ΔsaeRS group (Fig. S5C, D). These findings suggest that although fnbA/B are essential for synovial aggregation, other saeRS-regulated genes also contribute to pathogenesis.

S. aureus fak activates saeRS and fnbA/B by scavenging exogenous fatty acids
We subsequently tested how saeRS-fnbA/B responds to the human environment. By analysing the meta-transcriptome data of specimens from patients with S. aureus musculoskeletal infections, we observed higher read counts mapping to the fnbA/B locus in the JI group than in the N-JI group (Fig. 4A). Similarly, when S. aureus was cultured in vitro with SF or serum, upregulation of saeRS-regulated adhesins was observed (Fig. 4B–D and Supplementary Data 6). The upregulation of saeRS-regulated adhesins was more significant in SF than in serum, indicating that saeRS was in an active state within the joint environment.

We hypothesized that fak controls the saeRS-fnbA/B axis in SF. First, we detected no change in the transcription of fakA or fakB1/2 when the cells were incubated with SF (Fig. S5A). The transcription level of saeRS-fnbA/B in response to SF was subsequently compared between the WT and ΔfakA strains, and no difference was detected for the response of the ΔfakA strain to SF (Fig. 4E), suggesting that the upregulation of saeRS observed in synovial fluid is abrogated in the fak mutant. To further explore this phenomenon, we used C-13-labelled oleic acid and acetic acid to trace exogenous (fak) and endogenous fatty acids synthesis pathway (FASII) activity among the high- and low-aggregating strains, respectively; higher fak activity was detected among the high-aggregate strains (Fig. 4F–G). This result implies that differences in fak activity might lead to differences in aggregation ability among clinical strains. Upon comparative analysis of FakA/B1/B2 and SaePQRS protein sequences retrieved from 500 S. aureus strains deposited in public databases, we observed a high degree of polymorphism in FakA amino acid sequences, whereas the SaePQRS and FakB1/2 amino acid sequences were relatively conserved (Figs. 4H and S7). Furthermore, sequencing of our high/low-aggregating strains (H1–5 and L1–5) revealed amino acid polymorphisms with increased binding energy between FakA dimerization and FakA–FakB1 binding (Fig. 4I). Although the absolute binding energy provides little biological meaning, the relative values among strains are still helpful in elucidating the discrepancies in aggregation ability and Fak activity among clinical strains.

The biological function of fak is to exploit exogenous fatty acids (eFAs)15. To explore whether fak influences saeRS-fnbA/B through eFA, we treated S. aureus with common human fatty acids and found that eFA (oleic acid, palmitic acid, and myristic acid) inhibited saeRS-fnbAB transcription (Fig. S6B). We propose that fak, as a consumer of eFA, scavenges fatty acids, thereby alleviating their suppression of saeRS-fnbA/B. To further validate this model, we treated ΔfakA with fatty acid-free bovine serum albumin (FA-free-BSA) to scavenge intracellular fatty acids. A significant increase in sae activity was observed upon treatment of ΔfakA with FA-free BSA. (Fig. 4K). However, the rescue of sae transcription by FA-free-BSA was only partial compared with that of the wild type. This implies that other regulatory mechanisms are involved in the control of saeRS-fnbA/B by fak.

fak regulates SaeS activity by maintaining FMMs integrity
The mechanism by which fak regulates saeRS activity remains to be fully determined. Pathogens alter their cell membrane composition through the fak system to adapt to the host environment16,25. As SaeS is a membrane protein, it is likely influenced by changes in the cell membrane. FMMs, recently identified as crucial membrane structures, have been demonstrated to significantly influence the functionality of membrane-associated proteins26. A review of published FMM proteomic data27,28 revealed enrichment of SaeS in FMMs. Subsequent molecular dynamics simulations indicated potential binding between SaeS and FloA (scaffold protein of FMMs) within the cell membrane (Fig. S8A–D). This finding was confirmed in a bacterial two-hybrid (B2H) assay in which proteins were cloned as prey or bait in Escherichia coli (BTH101). The results revealed FloA–SaeS interactions but not with SaeP/Q (Fig. 5A–C). Furthermore, we performed a Co-IP experiment to verify the results in S. aureus. We first coexpressed USA300 with FloA-6×HIS and SaeS-3×FLAG. Then, FloA was precipitated using anti-HIS beads, and the precipitate was detected with an anti-FLAG antibody for SaeS. The results showed that FloA could bind with SaeS in S. aureus (Fig. 5D). To directly image the SaeS–FloA interaction in S. aureus, we split the mCherry protein, and the resulting N- and C-termini were labelled with FloA and SaeS, respectively, without impairing protein function (Fig. S9A, C, and D). Subcellular localization was observed with high-resolution confocal microscopy, and typical foci around the cell membrane were observed (Fig. S9B–C), indicating that SaeS and FloA interact at the FMMs.

Treating S. aureus with FMM inhibitors (zaragozic acid/ZA and simvastatin) resulted in the downregulation of sae activity (Fig. 5E, F). Moreover, the number of SaeS–FloA foci decreased when the cells were treated with FMM inhibitors (Fig. 5G), confirming the necessity of FMMs for saeS activity. We noticed that the FMM inhibitors were less effective in synovial fluid than in TSB (Fig. 5E, F) and that the FMM inhibitors could inhibit synovial aggregation only at high concentrations (Fig. 5H), where simvastatin started to display antibacterial effects (Fig. 5I). We next assessed the impact of fak on FMMs; the fakA mutant exhibited decreased or eliminated FMMs when grown in TSB and SF, respectively (Fig. S10). These results suggest that the ability of fak to modulate saeRS activity occurred through affecting FMMs structure (illustrated in Fig. 5J).

Metabolite screening reveals undecanoic acid as an inhibitor of the Fak system
Because fak activity is closely linked with eFA, it is hypothesized that eFA or its derivatives may affect the activity of the fak pathway. We tested 124 fatty acid metabolites and derivatives for their ability to inhibit aggregation (Supplementary Data 7), aiming to identify specific Fak–SaeRS inhibitors. Six metabolites significantly inhibited synovial aggregation (Fig. 6A–C), including itaconic acid (ITA) and its derivatives. Itaconic acid has been previously reported to alter carbon flow, reduce fatty acids synthesis, and inhibit bacterial growth at high concentrations (>10–30 mM)29,30, potentially accounting for its aggregation-inhibiting mechanism (Fig. S11). Among the other metabolites, linoleic acid (LA) is a known FASII inhibitor (FabI)31, and UDA has been reported to inhibit fatty acid synthesis in fungi32, although the exact mechanism remains unclear. Studies of 3b-hydroxy-5-cholenoic acid (HCA) have not been reported. S. aureus treated with LA and HCA inhibited growth, demonstrating antimicrobial effects (Fig. 6D). All the metabolites except HCA inhibited sae and fnbAB transcription to varying degrees (Fig. 6E).

To investigate the effects of these candidate compounds on S. aureus fatty acid metabolism, we used C-13-labelled oleic acid and acetic acid to trace exogenous and endogenous fatty acid pathways, respectively. Itaconic acid and its analogues inhibited endogenous FA synthesis but slightly increased the activity of the exogenous pathway. LA and UDA inhibited the endogenous and exogenous pathways, respectively. HCA inhibited endogenous fatty acid synthesis only at high concentrations (Fig. 6F, G).

UDA was the only identified metabolite that inhibited eFA incorporation in this study and exhibited a favourable IC50 (IC50 = 19.5 µM; Fig. 6H). Given the structural similarity of UDA to fatty acids, which are natural substrates for FakB1 and FakB2, we hypothesized that these proteins are the binding targets of UDA. Computational docking of FakB1/2 with UDA or fatty acids revealed favourable binding energy between FakB1/B2 and UDA; MD simulation revealed that UDA forms a stable binding complex with FakB1. Additionally, the RMSF results revealed low values for key residues (FakB1: ILE94, LEU160, and PHE263; FakB2: ILE118, THR259, ILE263, and GLY273), which were also predicted by molecular docking (Fig. S12B–D). Moreover, we adopted surface plasmon resonance (SPR) to investigate the direct binding of UDA with FakB1/2 (Fig. 6I). UDA bound FakB1/2 with an affinity similar to those of its natural ligands (myristic acid-FakB1, oleic acid-FakB2).

To evaluate its efficacy against clinical isolates, we assessed the effects of UDA on fak activity, sae and fnbAB transcription, and synovial aggregation among high-aggregating clinical strains. The results revealed significant inhibition across all the strains tested, even after continuous treatment for 14 days (Fig. S13A–C), underscoring its broad applicability to clinical strains.

UDA coadministration prevents anti-FASII antibiotic resistance and alleviates septic arthritis in mice
Because UDA does not exhibit antibacterial properties, we explored its potential as an antibiotic adjuvant for infection treatment. We tested combinations of UDA with gentamicin, vancomycin, and AFN1252 in culture media supplemented with SF or eFA. The results revealed that UDA enhanced the performance of AFN1252 under both eFA and SF conditions, whereas the efficiency of vancomycin and gentamycin was enhanced only in SF (Fig. 7A–C). AFN1252 inhibits FASII activity, making it an attractive target for antibiotic development33. The fak system is reported to be the cause of anti-FASII antibiotic treatment failure34. We explored whether UDA could hinder the occurrence of anti-FASII resistance. The results revealed that resistance emerged at a frequency of approximately 10−6 in the presence of synovial fluid or exogenous fatty acids, similar to the findings of a previous study35. However, when UDA was introduced, the frequency decreased by 4.68–32.5-fold (Fig. 7D–F). Continuous exposure to low-dose UDA and anti-FASII increased anti-FASII resistance, whereas UDA effectiveness was not impaired (Fig. 7G), suggesting that resistance to UDA is not readily developed.

We further investigated the efficacy of UDA for in vivo application. The initial assessment of biocompatibility revealed no significant impairment in macrophage or fibroblast viability (Fig. S14A, B). Intra-articular injection in a murine model did not result in liver or kidney damage, as confirmed by both histological and biochemical analyses (Fig. S14C–F). In a murine model of septic arthritis (Fig. 7H), the bacterial load was lower in the vancomycin group than in the AFN1252 group at 2 weeks post-treatment. When UDA was coadministered with AFN1252, the treatment efficiency was enhanced, and the treatment efficiency was comparable to that of vancomycin. Accordingly, the combination of UDA with AFN1252 resulted in favourable bacterial clearance, alleviation of local inflammation, removal of bacterial clumps, and recovery of joint function (Figs. 7I, J, L and S15A–C). We also tested the efficacy of UDA in treating the high-aggregating clinical isolates; the results revealed a significant reduction in bacterial load (Fig. 7K). Taken together, these data demonstrated that UDA could enhance the efficacy of AFN1252 in treating septic arthritis.
